sea.e: From Middle English see, from Old English sǣ, from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi (“body of water”), from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz, itself either: Derived from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂ey-wo- (“to be fierce, afflict”). Derived from Proto-Germanic *sīhwaną (“to percolate, filter”), from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ-.
sea.g: A large body of salt water.

seacoast.e: From Middle English see-cost, see-coste, see coost, equivalent to sea + coast.
seacoast.g: The coastal land bordering a sea or ocean.

seafaring.e: From Middle English safarinde, see farand, se farinde, equivalent to sea + faring (“travelling; journeying; going”).

seafaring.g: The act, process, or practice of travelling the seas, such as by sailing or steaming.

seah.g: A former Hebrew unit of dry volume, about 7.7 L or 7 quarts.

seal.e: From Middle English sel, from an inflectional form of Old English seolh, from Proto-West Germanic *selh, from Proto-Germanic *selhaz (compare Scots selch,selkie, North Frisian selich, Middle Dutch seel, zēle, Old High German selah, Danish sæl, Middle Low German sale, Icelandic selur), either from Proto-Indo-European *selk- (“to pull”).
seal.g: A pinniped (Pinnipedia), particularly an earless seal (true seal) or eared seal.

seal.e: From Middle English sel, sele, from Anglo-Norman seel, from Latin sigillum, a diminutive of signum (“sign”).
seal.g: A stamp used to impress a design on a soft substance such as wax.

seam.e: From Middle English sem, seem, seme, from Old English sēam (“seam”), from Proto-West Germanic *saum, from Proto-Germanic *saumaz (“that which is sewn”).
seam.g: A folded-back and stitched piece of fabric; especially, the stitching that joins two or more pieces of fabric.

seam.e: From Middle English seym (“grease”), from Old French saim (“fat”).

seamless.e: From Middle English seemles, semeles, semles, Old English *sēamlēas, equivalent to seam + -less.

sear.e: From Middle English sere, seer, seere, from Old English sēar, sīere (“dry, sere, sear, withered, barren”), from Proto-West Germanic *sauʀ(ī), from Proto-Germanic *sauzaz (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂ews- (“dry, parched”) (also reconstructed as *h₂sews-).

From Middle English seren, seeren, from Old English sēarian (“to become sere, to grow sear, wither, pine away”), from Proto-West Germanic *sauʀēn (“to dry out, become dry”); compare also Proto-Germanic *sauzijaną (“to make dry”). The use in firearms terminology may relate to French serrer (“to grip”).
sear.g: To char, scorch, or burn the surface of (something) with a hot instrument.

search.e: From Middle English serchen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sercher, Old French cerchier, from Late Latin circō, ,circāre (“to circle; go around; search for”), from circus. Unrelated to German suchen, which is cognate with English seek.

seashore.g: The coastal land bordering a sea or an ocean.

season.e: From Middle English sesoun, seson (“time of the year”), from Old French seson, saison (“time of sowing, seeding”), from Latin satiō (“act of sowing, planting”) from satum, past participle of serō (“to sow, plant”) from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow, plant”).
season.g: Each of the divisions of a year based on the prevailing weather: spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter; or the rainy (monsoon) and dry se
To flavour food with spices, herbs or salt.

seat.e: From Middle English sete, from Old English sǣte, possibly from (or simply cognate with) Old Norse sæti (“seat”), both from Proto-Germanic *sētiją (“seat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”); compare Old English set (“seat”).

seclusion.e: From Medieval Latin, from Latin seclusio, from secludere.
seclusion.g: The act of secluding, shutting out or keeping apart.

second.e: From Middle English secunde, second, secound, secund, borrowed from Old French second, seond, from Latin secundus (“following, next in order”), from root of sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
second.g: Number-two; following after the first one with nothing between them. The ordinal number corresponding to the cardinal number two.

second.e: From Middle French seconder, from Latin secundō (“assist, make favorable”).
second.g: To transfer temporarily to alternative employment.

secondarily.e: From Middle English secundarili. By surface analysis, secondar(i) + -ly.
secondarily.g: In a secondary manner or degree.

secret.e: From Middle English secrette, from Old French secret, from Latin sēcrētus (“separated, hidden”), from ptp of sēcernō (“separate, to set aside, sunder out”), from cernō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.

secretary.e: From Medieval Latin secrētārius (“one entrusted with secrets”), from Latin secrētus (“private, secret”), past participle of secernere (“to separate, set apart”), from se- (“apart”) + cernere (“to separate”).
secretary.g: A person who keeps records, takes notes and handles general clerical work.

sect.e: From Middle English secte, from Old French secte (“a sect in philosophy or religion”), from Late Latin secta (“a sect in philosophy or religion, a school, party, faction, class, guild, band, particularly a heretical doctrine or sect, etc.”), possibly, from Latin sequi (“to follow”).
sect.g: An offshoot of a larger religion or denomination.

section.e: From Middle English seccioun, from Old French section, from Latin sectiō (“cutting, cutting off, excision, amputation of diseased parts of the body, etc.”), from sectus, past participle of secāre (“to cut”).
section.g: A cutting; a part cut out from the rest of something.

secure.e: Borrowed from Latin sēcūrus (“of persons, free from care, quiet, easy; in a bad sense, careless, reckless; of things, tranquil, also free from danger, safe, secure”), from sē- (“without”) + cūra (“care”); see cure.
secure.g: Free from attack or danger; protected.

security.e: From secure + -ity, from Middle English securite, from Middle French securité (modern sécurité), from Latin sēcūritās, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe, secure”), from sē- (“without”) + cūra (“care”); see cure. Similar to Latin sine cūrā (“without care, carefree”), which led to English sinecure.
security.g: The condition of not being threatened, especially physically, psychologically, emotionally, or financially.

sedition.e: From Old French sedicion, from Latin sēditiō (“sedition, discord”), from sēd- (“apart”) (an alternative form of sē-) + itiō (“going”).
sedition.g: Organized incitement of rebellion or civil disorder against authority or the state, usually by speech or writing.

seduce.e: Borrowed from Latin sēdūcō (“to lead apart or astray”), from sē- (“aside, away, astray”) + dūcō (“to lead”); see duct.
seduce.g: To beguile or lure (someone) away from duty, accepted principles, or proper conduct; to lead astray.

seducer.g: Someone who seduces, especially a man who seduces a woman.

seductive.e: From Latin sēduct-, past-participle stem of sēdūcere, + -ive.

see.e: From Middle English seen, from Old English sēon (“to see, look, behold, perceive, observe, discern, understand, know”), from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”).
see.g: To perceive or detect someone or something with the eyes, or as if by sight.

see.e: From Middle English se, see, from Old French see, sié (“seat, throne; town, capital; episcopal see”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”), referring to the bishop's throne or chair (compare seat of power) in the cathedral; related to the Latin verb sedēre (“to sit”).
see.g: A diocese or archdiocese: a region of a church, generally headed by a bishop or an archbishop.

seed.e: From see + -d (“past tense suffix; variant of -ed”).

seedtime.e: From Middle English seed tyme, from Old English sǣdtīma (“time for sowing, season”), from Proto-West Germanic *sādatīmō, from Proto-Germanic *sēdatīmô (“seedtime”), equivalent to seed + time.

seeing.e: Probably an elision of "seeing that" or "seeing as".
seeing.g: Inasmuch as; in view of the fact that.

seek.e: From Middle English seke, seken, from Old English sēċan, sēċean, sœ̄ċan, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną (“to seek”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂gyeti (“to seek out”), from *seh₂g- (“to follow, trace”). The Middle English and later Modern English hard /k/ derives from Old English sēcð, the third person singular.
seek.g: To try to find; to look for; to search for.

seem.e: From Middle English semen (“to seem, befit, be becoming”), from Old Norse sœma (“to conform to, beseem, befit”), from Proto-Germanic *sōmijaną (“to unite, fit”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one; whole”).
seem.g: To appear; to look outwardly; to be perceived as.

seeming.g: Appearing to the eye or mind (distinguished from, and often opposed to, real or actual).

seemly.e: From Middle English semly, semely, semelich, from Old Norse sœmiligr (“seemly”); equivalent to seem + -ly.
seemly.g: Of behavior, appropriate; suited to the occasion or purpose; becoming.

seen.g: Indicates comprehension on the part of the speaker.

seer.e: From Middle English seere, equivalent to see + -er (“agent suffix”).
seer.g: One who foretells the future; a clairvoyant, prophet, soothsayer or diviner.

seething.e: From Middle English sethyng; equivalent to seethe + -ing.
seething.g: Filled with unexpressed anger; in a state of being livid.

seize.e: Earlier seise, from Middle English seisen, sesen, saisen, from Old French seisir (“to take possession of; invest (person, court)”), from Early Medieval Latin sacīre (“to lay claim to, appropriate”) (8th century) in the phrase ad propriam sacire, from Old Low Frankish *sakjan (“to sue, bring legal action”).
seize.g: To deliberately take hold of; to grab or capture.

seldom.e: From late Middle English seldom, alteration of earlier selden by analogy with adverbial datives such as whilom, from Old English seldan (“seldom”), from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā, from Proto-Germanic *seldanē.

select.e: From Latin sēlēctus, perfect passive participle of sēligō (“choose out, select”), from sē- (“without; apart”) + legō (“gather, select”).

self.e: From Middle English salve, self, silf, from Old English self, seolf, sylf, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”).
self.g: Himself, herself, itself, themself, themselves; that specific (person mentioned).

self-condemned.g: Condemned by one's own words, behaviour etc.

self-willed.e: From Middle English selfe-willed, selwillyd, equivalent to self- + willed.
self-willed.g: Obstinate; strong-minded; unyielding to the desires, concern or opinions of others.

selfish.g: Holding one's own self-interest as the standard for decision making.

selfsame.e: From Middle English self sam, self same, selve same (“the very same, selfsame”), from self (“that specific (person mentioned), herself, himself, itself, themselves”, pronoun) (from Old English self, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”)) + sam, same (“(adjective) equal, identical; unchanging; referred to earlier, abovenamed, aforementioned.
selfsame.g: Chiefly preceded by the: precisely the same; the very same; the same not only in being similar but in being identical.

sell.e: From Middle English sellen, from Old English sellan (“give; give up for money”), from Proto-West Germanic *salljan, from Proto-Germanic *saljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁-.
sell.g: To transfer goods or provide services in exchange for money.

sell.e: From French selle, from Latin sella.

seller.e: From Middle English seller, sellere, (also siller, sullar, sullere), from Old English *sellere, *syllere, equivalent to sell + -er (agent noun) (sense 1) and sell + -er (patient) (sense 2).
seller.g: Someone who sells; a vendor; a clerk.

semen.e: From Middle English semen, from Latin sēmen (“seed”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow; plant”).
semen.g: A sticky, milky fluid produced in male reproductive organs that contains the reproductive cells.

senate.e: From Middle English senat, from Old French senat, from Latin senātus (“council of elders; a senate”), from senex (“old”).
senate.g: In some bicameral legislative systems, the upper house or chamber.

senator.e: From Latin senātor, ultimately from senex (“old”), equivalent to senate + -or.
senator.g: A member, normally elected, in the house or chamber of a legislature called a senate, as, for instance, the legislatures of the United State

send.e: From Middle English senden, from Old English sendan (“to send, cause to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *sandijan, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sont-eye-ti (“to cause to go”), causative of *sent- (“to walk, travel”). The noun derives from the verb. Related also to Old English sand, sond (“a sending, mission, message”).
send.g: To make something (such as an object or message) go from one place to another (or to someone).

sense.e: From Middle English sense, from Old French sens, sen, san (“sense, perception, direction”); partly from Latin sēnsus (“sensation, feeling, meaning”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive”); partly of Germanic origin (whence also Occitan sen, Italian senno), from Vulgar Latin *sennus (“sense, reason, way”).
sense.g: Any of the manners by which living beings perceive the physical world: for humans sight, smell, hearing, touch, taste.

senseless.g: Without feeling or desire to work; deprived of sensation.

sensible.e: From Latin sēnsibilis (“perceptible by the senses, having feeling, sensible”), from sentiō (“to feel, perceive”).
sensible.g: Acting with or showing good sense; able to make good judgements based on reason or wisdom, or reflecting such ability.

sensual.e: From Late Latin sensualis (“endowed with feeling, sensual”), from Latin sensus (“feeling, sense”).

sensuality.e: From Middle French sensualité, derived from Late Latin sēnsuālitātem (“sensibility, capacity for sensation”). By surface analysis, sensual + -ity.
sensuality.g: The state of being sensual or sensuous.

sentence.e: Borrowed from Middle French sentence, from Latin sententia (“way of thinking, opinion, sentiment”), from sentiēns, present participle of sentiō (“to feel, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).
sentence.g: The decision or judgement of a jury or court; a verdict.

sentry.e: From earlier sentrie, sentery, of uncertain origin. Perhaps an alteration of sentinel or sanctuary; or perhaps from Old French senteret (“a path”), diminutive of sentier, from Medieval Latin semitarius (“a path”).
sentry.g: A guard, particularly on duty at the entrance to a military base.

separate.e: From Middle English separaten (“to separate”), from separat (“separated”) + -en, from Latin sēparātus, perfect passive participle of sēparō (“to separate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sē- (“apart”) + parō (“prepare”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).
separate.g: To divide (a thing) into separate parts.

separate.e: From Middle English separat (“separated”), from Latin sēparātus, see -ate (“adjective-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.
separate.g: Apart from (the rest); not connected to or attached to (anything else).

separation.g: The act of disuniting two or more things, or the condition of being separated.

sepulchre.e: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).

sequence.e: From Middle English sequence, from Old French sequence (“a sequence of cards, answering verses”), from Late Latin sequentia (“a following”), from Latin sequēns (“following”), from sequī (“to follow”); see sequent.
sequence.g: A set of things next to each other in a set order; a series.

seraphim.e: From Latin seraphim, from Koine Greek σεραφείμ (serapheím), from Biblical Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (śərāp̄îm), plural of שָׂרָף (śārāp̄) (often translated as "fiery ones" although meaning is uncertain); perhaps related to the root שרף (“to burn”).

serious.e: From Middle English seryows, from Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, an extension of Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”). (If this root is correct, cognate with German schwer (“heavy, difficult, severe”), Old English swǣr (“heavy, grave, grievous”).
serious.g: Without humor or expression of happiness; grave in manner or disposition.

serpent.e: From Middle English serpent, from Old French serpent (“snake, serpent”), from Latin serpēns (“snake”), present active participle of serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. In this sense, displaced native Old English nǣdre (“snake, serpent”), whence Modern English adder.

servant.e: From Middle English servaunt, from Old French servant, from the present participle of the verb servir. Morphologically serve + -ant.
servant.g: One who is hired to perform regular household or other duties, and receives compensation. As opposed to a slave.

serve.e: From Middle English serven, from Old French servir, from Latin serviō (“be a slave; serve”), from Latin servus (“slave; servant”), which perhaps derives from Etruscan (compare Etruscan proper names 𐌔𐌄𐌓𐌅𐌉 (servi), 𐌔𐌄𐌓𐌅𐌄 (serve)), or from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“watch over, protect”).
serve.g: To provide a service (or, by extension, a product, especially food or drink).

service.e: From Middle English servise, from Old English serfis, from Old French servise (French service), from the verb servir, from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus (“servant; serf.
service.g: An act of being of assistance to someone.

service.e: Properly, the tree that bears sorb fruit, from Middle English serves, plural of serve (“sorb apple, serviceberry”), from Old English syrfe, from Vulgar Latin *sorbea, from Latin sorbus (“service tree”).

servile.e: From Middle English servyle, from Old French servil, servile, from Latin servīlis, from servus (“slave”). By surface analysis, serve + -ile.

serving.g: The act or process of serving.

servitor.e: From Middle English servitour, borrowed from Latin servītor, from servīre (“to serve”).
servitor.g: One who performs the duties of a servant.

servitude.e: From Middle French servitude, from Latin servitūdō, from Latin servus (“slave”). Equivalent to serve + -itude.
servitude.g: The state of being a slave; slavery; being forced to work for others or do their bidding without one's consent or against one's will, either

set.e: From Middle English setten, from Old English settan, from Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sodéyeti, causative of *sed- (“to sit”).

From Middle English set, sette, from Old English set (“seat, place of residence, camp, settlement, entrenchment, stable, pen”), from Proto-West Germanic *set (“seat”), from Proto-Germanic *setą (“seat”).
set.g: A punch for setting nails in wood.

setter.e: From Middle English settere, equivalent to set + -er. The hunting dogs are so named because when they scent the game, they set (that is, strike a certain stance).

settle.e: From a merger of two verbs: Middle English setlen, from Old English setlan (“to settle, seat, put to rest”), from Old English setl (“seat”) (compare Dutch zetelen (“to be established, settle”)) and Middle English sahtlen, seihtlen (“to reconcile, calm, subside”), from Old English sahtlian, ġesehtlian (“to reconcile”).

From Middle English settle, setle, setel, setil, seotel, from Old English setl (“that upon which one sits, a seat, a settle, a place to sit”), from Proto-Germanic *setlaz (“a seat; arm-chair”), representing Proto-Indo-European *sed-lo-, from *sed- (“sit”).

seven.e: From Middle English seven, from Old English seofon (“seven”), from Proto-West Germanic *sebun (“seven”), from Proto-Germanic *sebun (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ (“seven”).
seven.g: A numerical value equal to 7; the number following six and preceding eight.

sevenfold.e: From Middle English sevenfold, sevenefold, from Old English seofonfeald. Equivalent to seven + -fold.
sevenfold.g: Seven times as much; multiplied by seven.

seventeen.e: From Middle English seventene, from Old English seofontīene, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to seven + -teen.
seventeen.g: The cardinal number occurring after sixteen and before eighteen, represented in Roman numerals as XVII and in Arabic numerals as 17.

seventeenth.e: From Middle English sevententhe, seventethe, from Old English seofontēoþa, equivalent to seventeen + -th.
seventeenth.g: The ordinal form of the number seventeen.

seventh.e: From Middle English seventhe, sefte, from Old English seofoþa, from Proto-West Germanic *sebundō, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô. The -n-, lost in northern Proto-West Germanic, was later reinserted by analogy with seven, equivalent to seven + -th.
seventh.g: The ordinal form of the number seven.

seventy.e: From Middle English seventy, sevynty, from Old English hundseofontiġ, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą (“seventy”), equivalent to seven + -ty.
seventy.g: The cardinal number occurring after sixty-nine and before seventy-one, represented in Roman numerals as LXX and in Arabic numerals as 70.

sever.e: From Middle English severen, from Old French sevrer, from Latin separāre (“to separate”), from se- (“apart”) + parāre (“provide, arrange”).

several.e: From Anglo-Norman several, from Medieval Latin sēparālis, from Latin sēpar (“separate”). By surface analysis, sever + -al. Not related to severe or seven.

severe.e: From Middle French, from Latin severus (“severe, serious, grave in demeanor”).

severity.e: From Middle English severity, from Middle French severite (modern French sévérité), from Latin sevēritās. By surface analysis, severe + -ity.

sew.e: From Middle English sewen, sowen, from Old English siwian, seowian, seowan (“to sew, mend, patch, knit together, link, unite”), from Proto-Germanic *siwjaną (“to sew”), from Proto-Indo-European *syewH- (“to sew”).
sew.g: To use a needle to pass thread repeatedly through (pieces of fabric) in order to join them together.

sexual.e: Borrowed from Latin sexuālis. By surface analysis, sex + -ual.
sexual.g: Arising from the fact of being male or female; pertaining to sex or gender, or to the social relations between the sexes.
